questions.q: Name the old woman who guides the narrator in Ujjain and state one specific action she performs that demonstrates her intimate connection to the ancient structures.
questions.a: The text does not give her a personal name; she is referred to as the "वृद्धा स्त्री" (old woman) who sits on the threshold ("नसग्जह") of a house in the ancient quarter. She demonstrates her connection by offering to unlock and show the narrator around the ancient courtyard house ("मकान") and by knowing the history of the lane ("गली") and the excavation. A wrong answer would invent a name (e.g., "Meera") or confuse her with the archaeologist — revealing the student treats her as a fictional character rather than a textual figure.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the narrator describes the archaeologists (Cunningham and the Indian team) as "supporting characters" in the story of Ujjain's rediscovery, rather than as the main discoverers.
questions.a: The archaeologists provide the *scientific validation* (stratigraphy, inscriptions, dating) that confirms Ujjain's antiquity, but the narrator frames them as latecomers: the city was never truly "lost" to its inhabitants — the old woman and her neighbors already lived atop the layers. The archaeologists' excavation merely made the *academic world* acknowledge what locals already embodied. A wrong answer would say "they discovered the city" — missing the text's irony that the city was continuously inhabited, so "discovery" is a colonial/academic construct.

questions.q: The narrator says: "क्या प्राचीन उज्जयिनी की नगरी नियोजन में भी उतनी ही दक्षता थी जितनी उसकी कला में?" (Was ancient Ujjain's town planning as skilled as its art?). Using the description of the excavated houses ("x<+" area), identify *two* specific planning features mentioned in the text and state which supporting character's perspective reveals them.
questions.a: Features: (1) Houses built on a grid with main streets running North-South and East-West ("उत्तर-दक्षिण और पूर्व-पश्चिम"), (2) Uniform brick size (1:2:4 ratio) and standardized drainage ("नालियाँ") opening onto main streets. These are revealed through the *archaeologists' excavation reports* (the "supporting character" of the archaeological team) which the narrator cites. A wrong answer would attribute this to the old woman or the narrator's imagination — confusing oral/local knowledge with archaeological evidence.

questions.q: Compare the "voice" of the old woman guide (who says "यहाँ कोई भी घर मुख्य सड़क पर नहीं खुलता") with the "voice" of the archaeological report (which describes "समान ईंटें, नियोजित नालियाँ"). What does this contrast tell you about the two ways of *knowing* the city?
questions.a: The old woman's voice is *embodied, experiential, and spatial* — she knows the city by living in its lanes, moving through thresholds, feeling the coolness of courtyards. The archaeological voice is *abstract, measured, and planar* — it knows the city through grids, ratios, and stratigraphic layers. The contrast shows that "heritage" is not a single truth: it is both a lived, sensory continuity (the woman) and a documented, analyzable past (the report). A weak answer would merely say "one is local, one is scientific" without explaining *how* each way of knowing shapes the narrator's (and reader's) perception.

questions.q: The narrator invokes Vikramaditya and Kalidasa as "characters" in Ujjain's story. Evaluate: does treating historical/literary figures as *supporting characters* in a travelogue strengthen or weaken the chapter's argument about living heritage? Justify with one textual example.
questions.a: It *strengthens* the argument — but only because the narrator does not treat them as remote myths. He places them *inside* the physical spaces the supporting characters inhabit: Kalidasa's "Meghaduta" cloud messenger flies over the *same* hills the narrator sees; Vikramaditya's court is linked to the *same* excavated palaces. The old woman's lane ("गली") becomes a bridge between 4th-century poetry and 21st-century bricks. A wrong answer would say "it's just decoration" — missing that the text uses these figures to collapse temporal distance, making heritage *palpable*.

questions.q: Write a 50-word "character sketch" of the *collective ancient inhabitant* of Ujjain (the "जनता" who lived in the excavated houses) using *only* inferences from the archaeological details in the text (brick ratios, drainage, courtyard layout, absence of main-door openings). Do not invent names or stories.
questions.a: A disciplined, privacy-valuing urban community that standardized construction (1:2:4 bricks), engineered city-wide drainage, oriented homes inward around courtyards rather than outward to streets, and maintained this order across centuries — suggesting strong civic norms and shared aesthetic-practical principles. A poor answer would project modern sentiments ("they loved their families") or vague praise ("advanced civilization") without anchoring each trait in a specific textual detail.
